opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm pretty uncertain, and the uncertainty is mostly about a few specific questions rather than a vague sense that "it might or might not work."

The first question is how far you need to scale before a model is competent enough across the full range of things a worker does. If you look at the loss curves and at how capabilities have shown up as models get bigger, you can extrapolate something like "with another few orders of magnitude of effective compute, you get a model that's quite smart on short, well-specified tasks." That part I feel moderately confident about. What's less clear is how much of a job is made up of those short tasks, versus things that require long-horizon coherence: keeping track of a project over weeks, noticing when you've gone off the rails, learning on the job from a small amount of feedback the way a new employee does.

So the second question, which I think is the crux, is about horizon length. How long a stretch of behavior do you need to train on before the model learns to do the long-horizon parts well? If you mostly need to train on short episodes, scaling plus fine-tuning gets you there relatively cheaply. If you need lots of data from tasks that take days or months, the effective cost of training goes up a lot, and that could push timelines out significantly. My guess is it's somewhere in between. A lot of long-horizon competence seems to come from composing short-horizon skills, plus some scaffolding, but I wouldn't be shocked if there's a real bottleneck there.

The third question is about the stuff around the model: tooling, integration, reliability. Even if a model is roughly as capable as a human on average, it's not a drop-in replacement if it fails in weird ways 5% of the time and nobody trusts it. In practice I expect a period where these systems are enormously useful as assistants and accelerate a lot of work before they're full replacements for a worker in the sense of "you just hand it the job."

If you made me put numbers on it, I'd say something like a meaningful chance, maybe 15-25%, that we have systems that can do most remote cognitive work by around 2030, and a substantially higher chance by the late 2030s. The thing I'd watch for is whether models start being able to do multi-day projects with minimal supervision. That's the empirical signal that would move me most, more than benchmark scores on any particular exam.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives a 15–25% chance of systems doing most remote cognitive work by 2030, but does not assign roughly 50% to the specified five-orders-of-magnitude compute scenario or deployment effort across many jobs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AI training through short episodes, scaling, and fine-tuning with human learning on the job from limited feedback.

r003.rationale: It says that even a model roughly as capable as a human may not be a drop-in replacement because tooling, integration, and reliability remain concerns.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't know, and I think the right way to think about it is mostly in terms of probabilities and in terms of what evidence would update you.

The way I'd frame it is: there's a question of how much more scaling buys you, and there's a separate question of how far away a drop-in replacement actually is in terms of the capabilities you'd need. On the first question, I think the trend over the last several years has been pretty remarkable. Each generation, you put in something like an order of magnitude more compute, you make the models bigger, you train on more data, and you get systems that are qualitatively more capable in ways that were hard to predict in advance. GPT-4 is doing things that if you'd described them to me in 2018 I would have said were quite a ways off. So the base rate for "scaling keeps delivering" is pretty good.

On the second question, I think the gap is bigger than it looks when you just chat with the model. A drop-in replacement for a human worker isn't just something that can answer questions well. It's something that can take a vague goal, operate over days or weeks, notice when it's confused, go find the information it needs, coordinate with other people, learn on the job, and not make the kind of mistake where it confidently does something crazy that no competent human would do. Current models are weak on a lot of that. They're very good at the "produce a plausible output for this prompt" part and comparatively bad at the long-horizon, self-correcting, agentic part.

So when I ask "will the next couple of orders of magnitude get us there," I'd put a meaningful probability on it, maybe something like a third, maybe a bit less, that the scaling trends plus the obvious algorithmic improvements plus a lot of engineering around the models gets you to something that can do most knowledge work by the end of the decade. And I'd put substantial probability on it taking a lot longer, because some of those capabilities, especially the long-horizon stuff and the robustness stuff, might turn out not to just fall out of predicting text better, and you might need qualitatively different training or a lot more RL on actual tasks.

The things I'd watch to update are pretty concrete. Can models do tasks that take humans a day rather than an hour? Can they do them without a human checking every step? Do the error rates on multi-step work come down fast or slowly? If I see that improving on the same kind of trend line as benchmark performance, I get more bullish. If it stalls while the benchmarks keep going up, that tells me the hard part is somewhere else.

And I'd add, I think even the uncertain version of this is a big deal from a safety standpoint. A one-in-three chance of something that can replace most human labor within ten years is not a thing you should treat as business as usual. So even though I'm uncertain, I don't think the uncertainty is a reason to relax.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives roughly a one-third chance of AI doing most knowledge work by the end of the decade, but does not discuss five orders of magnitude more effective compute or the probability that substantial deployment work would still be needed.

r002.rationale: It mentions that models may need to learn on the job, but does not distinguish how AI learns through fine-tuning from how humans learn on the job.

r003.rationale: It mentions engineering around models, but does not state that substantial workflow integration may remain necessary even if AI is as capable as humans.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate two questions. One is whether the same basic approach—training larger models, on more data, with more compute—can eventually get you there. The other is whether you get there just by making the next language model bigger, without changing how you train it to do useful work. I’m much more confident in the first claim than the second.

A drop-in replacement for a human needs to do more than give good answers to questions. You need to be able to hand it a task, have it figure out what information it’s missing, ask for clarification, and work on it for a long time. And when something goes wrong, it needs to notice and recover. There’s a big difference between being able to do each individual step of someone’s job and reliably doing the whole job.

So I’d want to look at how those abilities improve as we scale, and as we train models on tasks that actually require them. Can they complete longer projects with less supervision? Can they learn the particular things they need to know in a new workplace? How much human intervention do they require?

If a model fails at those things today, that’s evidence about what we can deploy today. It’s harder to know how much evidence it is about a fundamental limitation of the approach. Maybe there’s an important missing ingredient. Maybe we just haven’t put much training effort into the behavior we want. My expectation is that scaling will take us a substantial part of the way, but I wouldn’t treat performance on short questions as enough to establish that we’re about to replace human workers.

r001.rationale: The response gives no probability estimate or five-orders-of-magnitude compute comparison, and does not state that substantial deployment work across many jobs will remain necessary.

r002.rationale: It discusses training models on work-relevant tasks and learning workplace-specific information, but does not distinguish AI fine-tuning from human on-the-job learning.

r003.rationale: It mentions supervision and human intervention, but does not say that workflow integration may require substantial effort even if AI is as capable as humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two questions that are useful to separate. One is whether the models get smarter as you scale them up. The other is whether being smarter in the ways we currently measure is enough to do somebody’s job.

A model can know more than a human and be better at solving a problem once you’ve stated it clearly, while still being much worse at taking a vague objective and working on it for a week. A lot of the economic value depends on that second thing: noticing when you’re confused, gathering the information you need, checking your work, and recovering when something goes wrong.

So I’d want to look at how the length and complexity of tasks a model can reliably complete changes with scale. Can it do something that takes a human five minutes? An hour? A day? And how much human supervision does it need? If those numbers are improving consistently, that would be much stronger evidence than improvements on short questions.

My guess is that scaling will get us a substantial part of the way there, but I’m uncertain how much additional work is needed to turn those capabilities into a reliable worker. There could be a world where the underlying model is capable enough and it takes a few years to figure out the training and scaffolding. That would still be a very big deal, but it’s different from saying that you train the next model and immediately have a drop-in replacement for a human.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty and says training or scaffolding may take years, but gives no roughly 50% probability or five-orders-of-magnitude compute condition.

r002.rationale: It does not compare AI fine-tuning with human learning on the job.

r003.rationale: It says a capable model may still need work on training and scaffolding, but does not clearly state that substantial effort to integrate it into job workflows may remain necessary.
